utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We're back to work, back to normal. Before we -- I deal with the matter I prepared, I wonder whether there's anything to be raised by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning. First of all, I would like to introduce Vincent Le Junter, who is a legal intern working on our team who will be present during the first session this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson. Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Secondly, Mr. President, we have filed this morning a motion for modification of protective measures for the next witness, KDZ-555, and we have done that in another case. It's a confidential filing because we were advised yesterday by the Prosecution's notification that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, Mr. Robinson. I will come to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are seized -- shall we go into private session? I think it's safe to deal with everything in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. Before bringing the next witness, I understand there's one matter that you, Mr. Robinson, wanted to raise in relation to the scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. One matter we do have in mind, and I alerted the Chamber to this earlier, was the possibility of having one week in October so that we could organise ourselves to conduct some interviews that I have to conduct, myself, in Canada and also to give Dr. Karadzic and our team a little bit of a break between now and the time we have our winter recess. So we ask that the Chamber consider taking one week in October off so that we can accomplish those things without any disruption down the road to our continuing preparation for our Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has that been notified to the Prosecution? If I can hear from you on this matter, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We did receive an indication that the Defence would be bringing such a matter to the attention of the Chamber, and we didn't take a position on it. So we -- and that remains. We're in the Trial Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll let the parties know in due course very soon. Then we need to draw the curtains in order to bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we can begin doing that. But while we are doing that, I wanted to also ask the Trial Chamber to consider hearing this witness viva voce as opposed to pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In the witness's prior statement, he has basically signed a statement from 2008, but subsequently in two trials he's indicated that statement was not complete and has expressed some reservation about the accuracy of that statement. So in light of those concerns that he has expressed himself, we think that -- and in light of the history of his testimony and statements that have been made with the Office of the Prosecutor, we believe that it's best that he testify viva voce and that the statement not be considered as substantive evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters would kindly like to ask not to perform any proceedings while there is noise from the curtains going down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's wait. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I can respond before the witness is brought in to that. I think that would be jumping the gun a bit and it's really only half of the story. The witness's statement was accepted (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask to redact line 5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, if the audio-video unit could show the image of the witness, how he is seen in the monitor. You will be seen like this, Mr. Witness. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could first show the witness the pseudonym sheet, which is 65 ter -- oh. Actually, the pseudonym sheet's not uploaded yet, so I'll do it a different way. If we could please bring up in the Serbian language 65 ter 22781, which should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we still on Sanction or something? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, without saying your name out loud, reading this first page of this statement in your language, can you confirm that your name is written on the front page as the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we now go to the last page of the document. And the -- is that your signature, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, do you recall that you met me for the first time recently on 26 July of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at that time, did I provide you with a copy of the statement we've just seen in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall that you read the statement and then had some comments on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall that you had a clarification to the last page, the last paragraph, I should say, of the statement, and that other than that, you had no other corrections or clarifications to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now, then, is -- well, subject to the clarification that you made which we will do in a moment here in court, can you confirm that you still have no alterations, changes, corrections to the statement, that it's accurate and that if you were asked about the same topics, the information you provide us today would be the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed this statement two years ago. The Prosecutor has extracted the things that were needed by you. It is true what I said, but the statement does not reflect what I said. In other words, you have used only the things and portions that you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... but is it correct that you reviewed the statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But it's correct that you did review the statement paragraph by paragraph and sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I understand that this statement does not contain everything you've said to the Prosecution and does not contain everything you said during the making of the statement, but are the contents of the statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What was taken is correct, but it was taken out of context, but it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you stand by the statement and would give the same information today if asked on the same questions, albeit with additional comments or additional clarifications or points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all that I said is clear to you, but if the Court needs to understand everything that was happening, I think a clarification is necessary. The statements are summarised, and perhaps they require clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, what I would propose -- sorry, Your Honours. What I would propose at this time is to admit the statement, ask the witness to make the clarification he has to the one paragraph, 114, that he's identified, and I think as in previous times, any additional issues may be clarified during the cross-examination and much briefer direct which I would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I hear from you, Mr. Robinson, Mr. Witness, sir, you said like this: The Prosecution has used only the things and portions that the Prosecution was interested in, and what is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is taken is correct, but it was taken out of context while it is correct. Can you give me one or two examples so I can understand what happened, some concrete -- in some concrete sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, I don't know the exact item, but it deals with arming. Did you arm yourselves? I said, Yes. But before that, I explained the whole history, when we established the formation, when the Muslims started arming, what the videos were, and then they asked, Did you arm yourselves? I said, Yes. Another examples would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. Technical problem. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second problem is that about ten people from the OTP spoke to me from 2002 to today. And during that time they would change, and everybody had -- well, I don't know. When you speak to somebody from the OTP, they do not differentiate between Mali Zvornik, Veliki Zvornik, while that is very important to us. Another thing that is very important for the accused or for the indictment is that our whole lives we were getting by because we knew about that agreement with Holbrooke, and we thought that he would never be charged, and we thought he could help us at the local level in the community and it cannot do any harm. So perhaps I mentioned him in some context which was not quite accurate in view of the fact that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could locate -- let us know the passage where he's referred to Mr. Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There's none in the statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think what the witness is referring to is the fact that he's -- because what he understood to be the situation, he said some things about Dr. Karadzic that may not have been accurate, thinking that Dr. Karadzic would not be brought before a court because of the Holbrooke agreement, not that he had said anything about the Holbrooke agreement in his statement. That's my understanding. You could confirm that with the witness, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I may say, Your Honour, the -- the mention of Dr. Karadzic in paragraph 114 is exactly what the witness clarified to me and found is the only thing which he wanted to change in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I hear you now, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If you look at the text of Rule 92 ter (A)(3), it requires that the witness attest that the written statement or transcript accurately reflects the witness's declaration and what the witness would say if examined. And I think it's clear here that the second part of it has not been met, that this is not what the witness would say if examined, that he wants to add context to it. He says some parts of it were inaccurate. It doesn't accurately -- while it may be accurate in part, it does not accurately reflect what he would say if examined, and I think the requirements of Rule 92 ter are not met in this case. And I also think, just as a matter of fairness and as a matter of the Trial Chamber's discretion, that it would be safer to hear the witness's testimony viva voce so you can understand what his position is more accurately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to reply, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just this, Your Honour: I think that the witness has not said the statement is inaccurate. What the witness has said is that it's not everything he would say on every topic, and that it's -- if he spoke about these things viva voce, there would be more. That's almost always true, but I think the requirement has been met, that he would -- that what is in this statement is accurate. He would say these things. He might say more but that the Rule has been met in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just in case, I'm asking you, how much time would you need if required to lead him in viva voce?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry to say I'm not sure what an accurate estimate would be. It would be, I think, at least a day, probably more, and there's no -- there's no mystery. If I lead him viva voce, what I will do is -- is intend to do is go through the -- essentially, the entire statement and would go through the same order and go through these points. So it would take quite a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber carefully reviewed the words of Rule 92 ter, as well as what the witness said. Although the witness was not able to give some concrete examples, the witness clearly said that, "The statement does not reflect what I said." In light of this answer of the witness, the Chamber is not satisfied that the requirements of Rule 92 ter has been satisfied. So I order you to lead evidence live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go through your testimony now. Please remember that you've been reminded before to be careful about what you say so that you don't, unintentionally yourself, compromise your protective measures. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we will be careful to avoid in public testimony points which would identify you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Witness. Whenever you are going to say anything that may reveal your identity, please let us know that we go into private session in order to protect your identity. Do you understand that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. We all follow that. We know all the witnesses who come. This is just because of the name and the face, because of the work that I'm doing in a different town, but people are just not interested any more in what happened before and what's going on now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, Witness. Earlier, we talked just a little bit about -- well, strike that. I want to ask you now a little bit about the background in Zvornik in 1991 and your view of the situation building up to the -- to the outbreak of the armed conflict. So can you tell us quickly what you recall of the approximate population breakdown in Zvornik in 1991, early 1991, between different ethnic groups, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, because we took part in the census at the time, the Muslim population accounted for 60 per cent of the population. The Serb population accounted for about 40 per cent. There were about 1 or 2 per cent who declared themselves as Yugoslavs or Croats or some other minority. That caused some concern among us, because we used to have 55 per cent of the population in Zvornik, we the Serbs, according to the previous census. So we realised that people intentionally moved in, and also there is the traditional birth rate in the Islamic world, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, can you explain what the relationship was like between Muslims and Serbs in Zvornik before and after the 1991 elections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, while the strong fist of Communism was still there, inter-ethnic conflicts were punished severely. So the situation was good, under quotation marks. Quite simply, these were two parallel world. If I tell you that in my village which is a purely Serb village ethnically, no one ever married a Muslim. There was a river dividing us from a Muslim village, and no one ever had even a meadow on the other side. (redacted) and I never even went there for a dance or something, and they never came to my village either. So with Communist oppression, all of this was kept in peace, apparently. However, after the multi-party system was introduced, there was this explosion of inter-ethnic tensions that rose all the way until 1992 when the trigger was the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their separation from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, out of an abundance of caution, we should probably have a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And from your -- from your perspective as a member of the SDS then, what was the goal or position of what the SDS wanted at that time for Bosnia-Herzegovina before the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my personal motive for joining the SDS was to preserve Yugoslavia within its former framework. That was one of the main points of the SDS. Another thing, in view of the history in that part of the country, it had to do with the survival of myself and my family in this house where we were born and raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to December 1991. Did you attend any large SDS meetings that month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what date it was, but I think it was the end of December. I attended a meeting at the Holiday Inn where there were a lot of people, 500, 600, perhaps even more. For the most part, it was all the representatives of Serb people in the state organs, in the municipalities, members of parliament. All of them were invited. Since the SDS had most of the members there, but there were other people who represented the Serb people at municipal and republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall who was there from the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, all of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall Radovan Karadzic being there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall that the president spoke there at that meeting, and I think that Mr. Krajisnik spoke as well, and I think Professor Ekmecic, and I cannot remember who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Excuse me. To the best of your recollection, tell me what your recall Mr. Karadzic -- President Karadzic saying at that meeting. In other words, what was his speech about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he informed us about the situation at that moment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the political situation, also what the position of Bosnia was on an international plane and what the position of Serbia was. And basically what was discussed was the political situation and the attitude of the JNA towards this entire situation and the attitude of Yugoslavia towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the context, but for the most part, it had to do with providing information about the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was very difficult. I think that the parliament was about to disintegrate, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did Karadzic say about the situation regarding the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean I cannot remember exactly. It was about 20 years ago, but I think that it was that well-known situation that the Muslims were boycotting the JNA, that quite a few of them were not responding to call-up, and that the position of the Serbs was that we should promptly respond to JNA call-up because the war on Croatia was well underway already. So it was that variant. And the position of the JNA was at the time -- and I think that a reference was even made then. I don't know if it was Mr. Karadzic or somebody else, but the American embassy at the time officially supported the preservation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall Karadzic discussing whether he'd been in contact with President Milosevic about the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not remember whether he mentioned Mr. Milosevic then. Well, there were journalists there and they were reporting about it, and it can probably be seen from the newspaper reports at the time whether he did mention that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, earlier you were asked on this topic of what Mr. Karadzic had said at this meeting, and you explained what you've just said about the American ambassador, and you also said: "And he," Karadzic, "also had been to Belgrade and spoken to President Milosevic. And then we also had the support of the Serbian people to preserve the Yugoslavia, albeit truncated." Does that help you to remember what Dr. Karadzic said in his speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. It's been 20 years. I really cannot remember. I probably mentioned that in that case that you referred to, no problem with that, but, I mean, thinking of the consequences of this sentence, I mean, free interpretation remembering some meeting that took place 20 years ago and who said what, that would not be a normal thing, especially at that time I did not attach any importance to that meeting, and, I mean, I didn't realise there was anything important going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me just clarify that. This is a meeting with hundreds of people. You said who all the representatives were who were there. You said that you joined the SDS because of your concern about your people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you said there was talk about the JNA and support and what would happen. Let me ask you, are you -- did this have importance to you at that time? Did you attach any importance to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, believe me, it's the end of 1991. It was like the fastest movie you could imagine. I could not even count what was going on and what was more important than the other thing, but there were hundreds of things happening at local level and -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just let me ask again though. Out of these hundreds of things happening at very quick speed, was this meeting important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice a difference between that and other meetings except that this one was a more massive one, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Were any documents distributed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No documents were distributed to the participants. I did not receive a single document. But when I returned to Zvornik, I found out from the president of the SDS that he had received some document that later on we read together. It included an elaboration of some theses as to how one should behave in crisis situations. That was Variant A for municipalities where the majority population was Serb and Variant B for municipalities where Serbs were a minority. Later, as for the municipal variant, we looked at this paper and we assessed that it was something that was not bad for implementation in a community such as Zvornik was. And I think we corrected some things with regards to Variant B. We got rid of some things that we could not adopt but we did adopt some of it as a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how soon after this meeting was it you say when you returned to Zvornik? You found out from this document from the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a few days. Five or six days, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have P005 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now, looking at that document in your language, tell us what that is, please, if you've seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the instructions that I got from the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say the president of the party, could you say that person's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we resume, Mr. Robinson and Mr. Tieger, the Chamber has decided that it will take a week off in the week of 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If we could go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you please tell me -- take a look at this document adopted on 15 March 1992, so before the outbreak of hostilities is the date you've put on the armed conflict. The Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik adopted this decision regarding the ban on the sale of real properties. And if you look at item number I, I won't read the whole portion out, but these types of real property cannot be subject to trade except between ethnic Serbs within the municipal territory. And there is a similar clause under number VII regarding privately owned real estate between ethnic Serbs cannot be traded to other ethnic groups. Can you tell me about this decision. Why was this type of decision issued regulating the sale of property on an ethnic basis and prohibiting property from going outside of members of the Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember this decision. Since Zvornik has some specific features, a lot of Muslims lived in Serbia. Now, in the face of the heightened tensions, there emerged a huge influx of Muslims from Mali Zvornik and Sakaj [phoen] -- were swapping land with the Serbs. In fact, that only deteriorated and exacerbated the ethnic composition of Zvornik to the detriment of the Serbs. Now, given that the war in Croatia was in progress and that the situation was such that for three months Serbs were holding guard in their own villages, as did the Muslims, the Serbs did not dare enter any Muslim village and vice versa. So people were already divided on the ground. And under such extraordinary circumstances, we thought that it would not be good to engage in any swapping or sale of land given that the circumstances were so exceptional.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just let me clarify. This decision is from 15 March 1992. You're talking about the war being in process and for three months the Serbs were holding guard. Was the war in process on 15 March 1992 when this decision was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I said clearly that on the 15th of March there was no war, but I am telling you that before the war, the situation in Zvornik municipality was such that both the Serbs and the Muslims were armed. Three or four months before the war, the Serbian police could not enter any Muslim village or vice versa because that was the division on the ground, and that implied [as interpreted] guards for a few months before the outbreak of hostilities, because that was the factual situation on the ground. Everybody was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall, as you sit here today, whether this decision we've just been looking at was pursuant or in relation to the plan B as you're called it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer from the beginning. The interpreters couldn't understand him. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters were not able to hear your answer. Could you repeat it kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that was not in compliance with plan B, because I think that there is no mention in plan B of such provisions. This was our measure taken in Zvornik municipality in order to exert pressure on the incumbent authorities because we were disenfranchised, and we were put in the position of being in opposition. That was the situation at the local level. If you look at these plans A and B, they were never applied according to the same pattern in every municipality. It was different in each municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me ask you how you know, just so you can explain to us the way in which the Variant A and B instructions were applied in each municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We communicated with Ugljevik, Bijeljina, Bratunac, Srebrenica, neighbouring municipalities like Sekovici. All of them had their own respective patterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, sorry, who is the "we communicated"? Who's the "we" in that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to the representatives of the Serbs, representing them in the government organs, whether they were members of the SDS, of the League of Communists, or people from the party of Ante Markovic. All in all, those were the Serbs who held offices and who were elected at -- by the Serbs at the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... Your Honours, I would ask -- Your Honours, I'd ask to admit that -- or I tender that document, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up another document now quickly. That's 14639, please. And I would ask if we can just quickly show the witness the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've seen this before, sir. Could you tell us what this is, what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is another proof that Zvornik functioned as a state within a state. You can see here that it was the municipality paying out pensions, which is nowhere within it -- its remit. (redacted) (redacted) This has to do with the paying out of Serb pensioners who were receiving their remuneration through the Investbanka in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this document concerns the allocation of assets for pensions from April and states: "We ask you for the purposes of payment of pensions for April to the pensioners of Serb ethnicity, who receive their pensions through Investbanka ..." to enlarge it. Why is it, going back to April, there were only persons of Serbs ethnicities who are on this document to receive pensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're not right. This is dated the 17th of June and this is a backpay of these pensions that were due in April. On the 17th of June, there were no Muslims in Zvornik anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a backpay for April. That's my point. And there were no Muslims left in Zvornik by June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the payment is being made, according to the document, on the 17th of June. So they were about two months overdue. And on the 17th of June, no pensions could have been paid to the Muslims because none of them was physically present any longer in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you saw this document. I'll ask you: Did you see any similar documents authorising the paying of pensions to people of ethnicity other than Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me see -- let me ask you a question about your --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're in open session now, sir, so if you think we need to go into private session for a part of your answer, just tell me. You spoke earlier about the difficult ethnic tensions before the war, about every side arming themselves and about standing guard. I want to ask you now about your knowledge of the arming of -- of persons before the actual outbreak of the conflict. Now, first, which -- which groups were arming themselves, Muslims, Serbs, both, neither? Can you tell us who was arming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both were arming, and there was a race as to who would do it more successfully and better. They had their own methods, and that was Croatia, the front from the Croatian front where there were many volunteers on the side of Croatia. They were importing them from abroad, then the MUP was expanding. We had such a high number of the reserve forces, much more than the international standard was, and the Serbs used the JNA more. They would enlist in the JNA. They would use the fact that the Muslims were not enlisting, so they were filling up the reserve forces. And also there were other weapons issued from the Territorial Defence, but mostly the biggest source was the army, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just tell me if you have any knowledge about the arming by the Muslims in your area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, mostly it was from the Croatian front and through foreign purchases. I also mentioned the example that we received information as well as a tape that sometime in 1991, in October, I saw that they established the Patriotic League in the village of Godus and what surprised us very much at the time was that we saw about 100 armed persons dressed up to standards of NATO, wearing vests and with other equipment. And there was panic, and to this very day in this place of Horgos there is a monument saying that in October 1991 they formed this Patriotic League. So, for us, that was the starting shot for us to start pushing the army and people in Serbia who would be able to help us in this part of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, because there was a lull then with the Croats. There were no combat actions, so we used some private connections in Slavonia, Baranja, from Beli Manastir, and so on, to bring in the bulk of the weapons. Besides the fact that the army distributed weapons for the reserve forces through some personal connections, we brought weapons from Slavonia, Baranja, from Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter notes: We did not hear the second location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could repeat the second location. I think it must have been at the end of your answer. The interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was saying from Baranja it was from Darda and Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me just ask you one point on your -- on your last answer. Is your -- is your information that the Muslims were arming up to NATO standards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I'm just saying that we saw this video from the founding of the Patriotic League, and we could see the people there were dressed like members of a professional army. They had helmets, bullet-proof vests, automatic weapons, night vision equipment, communications equipment, just like any other professional army and special units at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I neglected to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. 14639 will be admitted as Exhibit P3152.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to private now and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. It's time to take a break. We will break for one hour and resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I -- could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in open session could you please describe to us what you remember of the way the attack on Zvornik took place from the beginning of who ordered the attack on how it commenced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack on Zvornik, as I said, was ordered by Arkan. His men, some 20 soldiers, took part in this attack. There were also some 100 volunteers, and another 100 or 200 people from the Zvornik TO and MUP. So I estimate that following Arkan's order, some 2- to 300 men launched an attack on Zvornik. (redacted) (redacted) And the conflict lasted from 4.00 or 5.00 until 8.00, and that makes it about three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you tell me the names that you remember of some of the volunteer groups that took part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not sure, because it's been a long time since then, but I think the Niski Pivarski were there, Zuco's group. There were some who said that they were from Vukovar, White Eagles. It's very difficult to know now who was there, you I think that there were about a hundred of these volunteers in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall if there was a group of volunteers called Gogic's group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was a group of volunteers from Loznica, yes. About ten people at the most from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did they take part in this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what -- what was the outcome of this action? What happened immediately after the attack ended, as you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outcome of the action was that about half of Zvornik was placed under the control of the Serbian side, all the way up to the department store. Then for the next 20 days or so, there was a part that was no man's land because it was controlled by firing up from Kula, and once Kula was placed under Serbian command, then practically all of Zvornik came under Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may request private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, Witness. What is the -- you've already stated these are what we refer to as the Variant A and B plan or instructions. What is the heading on the top left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It states: "The Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Main Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... what is the next -- what does the next writing on the document say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Strictly confidential, copy number 100."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. So did I understand you to say that this was an open document? It was openly discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how we treated it, and you can see that besides the Crisis Staff members there are also members from other parties there, the people from the SDA who were sitting in the offices next door knew about it. We didn't understand this to be particularly confidential or anything like that. Party post was delivered in a particular way. This was given by somebody to Grujic at a meeting at the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm going to move on. We can stay in public session. After the takeover of Zvornik, the attack, whatever we want to call it, how long did the Crisis Staff continue to function in that form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it was till the 20th of April, and then after the 20th of April, sometime the temporary government was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who, as best you recall, was the head of the temporary or interim government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Grujic was at the head of the provisional government, the temporary government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who were -- well, were any of the members who'd been on the Crisis Staff members of the provisional government? Any others, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some were part of the continuity, and they transferred from the Crisis Staff to the interim government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you name the persons you remember who were part of that continuity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Grujic, Radic, Peric. I'm not sure about any others. There is a list in the documents that was shown to me before, so perhaps they are in the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would be Stevo Radic and Rade Peric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were there any persons of Muslim ethnicity in the provisional government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember Mr. Muhamed Jelkic. He was a cardiologist from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was his role there? Was he voluntarily a member? Can you explain why he was a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think he was too enthusiastic about being a member of the interim government, but I think that he was one of the most respectable Muslims in Zvornik because he was from a good family. He was a cardiologist. He worked at the medical centre, and he enjoyed a good reputation among the Muslims and the Serbs, and this government tried to forge good links with the Muslim sides, and I think that he even participated in efforts to free a Serb policeman who was captured. He was a kind of link between the interim government and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who was the TO commander during the actual takeover of Zvornik, during the combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was Marko Pavlovic. At the beginning, there was some two or three shifts that lasted for a day or two. Some other people were mentioned, but I think that Marko Pavlovic was the TO commander from the point of time when Zvornik was attacked onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 17245, please. And page 37 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is -- this is a decision of the temporary or interim government, Serbian government of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik, on 10 April, appointing Marko Pavlovic, TO headquarters commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And whose name is at the bottom of the appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President of the interim government Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have Mr. Grujic's name in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't actually see it on the English. It is on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. It is a difficult format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the next page, yes. You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, at about this time did some members, in your words, of the Crisis Staff or provisional government quit and withdraw from that organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not take part in anything at the time, so I don't know what you're thinking of, so if you can remind me. I don't know exactly what you are thinking of. I wasn't participating in the work of the TO or the interim government at that time, or the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, do you recall Jovo Mijatovic and Jovan Ivanovic withdrawing from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They resigned and did not take part in all of that anymore. After being beaten by Arkan, they were very unhappy about that, and even for a while they suspected that somebody set them up from the Crisis Staff. So they withdrew. They were disappointed with what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified, for example, that the Crisis Staff financed the paramilitaries, that they were supported, they were given weapons by the provisional government and Crisis Staff when they arrived. How do you say -- is in that -- you say they have nothing to do with the provisional government, but you've explained even the way some of them were billeted and their accommodation paid for by the provisional government. Can you just explain it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. That is why I asked to testify live. What I stated is correct. The Crisis Staff was gathering volunteers, paying them. They were on a payroll. But I also explained that at one point in time these volunteers because the strongest armed force in Zvornik, and that it culminated to such an extent that there was an official proposal made that Zvornik should be named Zuca's town. Can you imagine that? It's as if seven or eight persons came to visit you at your home, they get drunk and they then start mistreating you and your children and everybody. You ask for help. Help did arrive, a bit late though, by way of a special unit from the MUP of Sarajevo reinforced by some other forces. They arrested them, but until that happened, by the time this information reached Pale, I said that there was no communication. Practically there was no communication. And by the time a reaction arrived from up there, ugly things had already happened. That's my answer to this question. Otherwise, let me just say that everyone in Zvornik knows that these paramilitaries, after all, the Muslims know this, too, they mistreated the president of the Crisis Staff. They took him out to execute him. He was a martyr, not a president of a Crisis Staff. Zuco, Captain Dragan both detained him, anyone who wanted to arrest him. Quite simply, from the time when Arkan came and until these paramilitaries were arrested, they were the strongest unit in Zvornik, and no one dared oppose them in any way, let alone not give them a salary or fuel or whatever, do anything against their wishes, what they had asked for. They wanted to attack Kalesija and they were using an engine that they wanted to transform into a train for that attack, and they used millions for it. Not to go into detail, but the culmination of this was that there was an official proposal in the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik that Zvornik be renamed into Zuca's town. Can you then imagine the environment that we lived in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So these groups of volunteers or paramilitaries that you're discussing, if I understood you correctly, they were invited by the Crisis Staff who paid for their transportation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, the Serbs who were a minority in Zvornik, asked all volunteers, I mean all of those who volunteered to come. We gave them weapons. They joined units. We put them on the payroll of the TO and that was the practice then. However, very soon they withdrew from the front line. They set up check-points on the road. They started seizing cars. They started checking people who were going in and out of town, because they had their own propaganda, too. They were not naive about any of this. They said, you know, The government is taking away your money. They're selling Muslims for money. They were saying millions of subversive things like that. This was some kind of negative marketing regarding the authorities. For a while they even had a lot of support amongst the population, you know, because when there's this kind of disbelief, it is fertile ground for rumours and misinformation. They used that skilfully. So along with the volunteers that came from elsewhere, quite a few of the locals from the TO joined these paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could I have 07136, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that document, sir, by Captain Dragan, who allegedly detained the president of the Crisis Staff together with Zuco, who did -- who did you refer to, Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think his name is Dragan Vasiljkovic. He operated in Croatia, and he came to us as "Captain Dragan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you just look at this document, sir. You've seen this before. Invoice dated 30th of April. Does this document indicate the provisional government paying for bringing volunteers from Belgrade to Zvornik, if we look at page 2 especially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about some of these groups joining the TO and their members. Did any particular volunteer/paramilitary group join the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, all of those who came were deployed in the Territorial Defence. But later on, I think it was in May, precisely in an attempt to stop these well-organised paramilitary groups, one group was admitted into the police. Since they were from Loznica, we knew them. They were neighbours from across the Drina. They joined the police in order reinforce it and precisely to put a stop to these organised groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the time I was not in the police or the Crisis Staff. This is what I know as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go through some of these documents -- some documents quickly, Witness, which relate to what you've just told us about the paramilitaries being paid, being put on the payroll of the provisional government, and the first one is 12159.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could this be made more specific? I have an objection. The government did not pay paramilitaries. The government paid volunteers in accordance with the law. It is only later that the volunteers became paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe that's matter for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. You can clarify with the witness. And it is the accused not the witness who intervened just before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see the English of 12159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to, I'm sorry, come back to that one. Could I have 14640, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can we go to the second page for the witness in Serbian. And continue on to page 6 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm showing you page 6 of a document entitled, "Payroll of unemployed reservists who were at the military exercise," and this is for the month of May, 1992, 1st of May, going on. First of all, do you see who signs this payroll?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On behalf of the TO staff, but then I'm not sure whose signature it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Does it say TO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks like Marko Pavlovic's signature, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he was -- and he was TO commander in May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we can scroll over to the left. Number 41, who is that gentleman listed as number 41 who is getting paid by Marko -- or who Marko Pavlovic is signing off for this man's pay in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vuckovic, Vojin Zuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... is that the same Zuca you were talking about earlier? Is that the same Zuca you were speaking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same one we were speaking about. I have already said that every volunteer who came was sent either to a TO unit or to the MUP, and they would pay such a person as a member of the TO. Until they became the strongest ones. Once they became the strongest ones, then they took whatever they wanted themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And who would send them to the TO and incorporate them into the TO as you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they would come, they would report to the Crisis Staff, to the provisional government, and then they would go directly to the TO, and then they would be deployed in accordance with their capabilities depending on what kind of military service they did, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and would I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, could I now have 13326, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this document is titled: "List of payments to be made to TO members of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik for the month of May." You've seen this document before. Just very quickly, is this another payroll for volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, but this is already annoying me, that I am supposed to comment on a document from May that you are showing me now? Bring someone from the government. I can just read it out as an announcer or whatever. This doesn't mean a thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, the reason is you already spoke about this document in your statement and said that you recognised it as a unit of the Serbian Radical Party led by Janko Lakic. That is why we're showing it to you at this point. Could I have 23235, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no comment. If you want me to read this out, I will read it out then. It is a list. The TO is paying a unit for the month of May, and I have no comment in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is part of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can explain. 23 -- 23235 is the remainder of the document shown to the witness that was in paragraph 78 of his statement that he commented on. Unfortunately, just the first two pages of this ERN range were originally included. So this is just -- although the statement is now not being admitted 92 ter, this -- these following pages are part of the same range the witness was shown for 23235 for -- sorry, P00159. And I've spoken with my friend who has no objection to these being shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm not trying to annoy you, but these are the remainder of the pages. Again, you don't need to comment more than this is another payroll certificate for volunteers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can just read it out like an announcer: "Certificate by which it is being confirmed that Boris Bosner received the following amounts as compensation for the payments to the Serbian municipality Zvornik --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to read it aloud. I'm just asking you if you know what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a certificate, and then I can read out what it says there. I don't see in which other way I can comment upon this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who is the first person named on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number one says Janko Lukic. That is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can see that it's -- we can see that there's a sort of handwritten correction to "Janko Lakic." Who was Janko Lakic? Did you know who Janko Lakic was in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it has to do with the Janko Lakic I know, this was a man who was born in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik. In 1991, he lived in Mali Zvornik. I don't know whether he was a volunteer or whether it was his duty to respond to a call up from this unit. Now, I don't know. The man was born in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik but I know that he lived in Mali Zvornik in Serbia as I did and many others. Now, whether he was a volunteer or he responded to a call-up from the TO, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would submit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would object because the witness hasn't really confirmed the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But his observation was that it was consistent with what he saw at the time before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That may be Mr. President, but with respect -- I don't want to say anything in open session that might reveal his identity, but the time-period makes a difference, in our view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if I may add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Judge, perhaps it seems that I have now started paying attention to details, because this is my fifth trial. Look at this document. There is no number here. There is no stamp. No one signed that they received this money. Commenting upon a document like this and saying anything about any of these people here, I think that is a thankless thing. As for what the Prosecutor asked me to do, I can read all of this out like an announcer, but I really have no knowledge of any of this. There is no stamp. There is no number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is sufficient, Mr. Witness. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, would you like to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honours, that the -- yes. Perhaps -- I don't think we need to go into private session. The witness said that he knew the first person named on the list, knew that he was from Serbia and was serving in a unit in the TO. So he does know about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, may I intervene? Unless there is a mistake in the translation, the witness did not say that he was from Serbia. The first person on the list is from Zvornik. He was born in Veliki Zvornik, but he lived in Mali Zvornik. He is not from Serbia. He just lived in Serbia, and that is the basis upon which he could have been a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the answer of the witness that he has no knowledge of this document, the Chamber is of the view that the Prosecution will have another opportunity to tender this. It's not appropriate to admit this document through this witness. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Thank you. For planning purpose, how much would you need for your remainder of your examination-in-chief tomorrow, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would -- I would try to finish in less than two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00, and it will be a normal sitting, not being an extended one. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.01 p.m.,
